title: Incident response: ransomware, lateral movement and memory
summary: Take a ransomware incident at an engineering firm from the first call to the executive summary: keep a chain of custody, rebuild the night from VPN, Windows, Sysmon and process logs, read memory-forensics and triage output, map every step to ATT&CK, decide under pressure in a tabletop, and write the report.
titlePrefix: Incident response: ransomware, lateral movement and memory
rubric: Evidence hashed and a chain of custody kept for every file you handled
Entry point found and backed by evidence: the VPN, the account and the missing MFA
Lateral movement reconstructed host by host, with times
Credential theft shown from the process tree and the memory output
Impact: what was encrypted, when, and which recovery options were destroyed
Timeline mapped to ATT&CK, one technique per step with its evidence
Executive summary a non-technical reader can act on, and a complete technical annex
handin: An executive summary, a technical annex and a lateral-movement timeline mapped to ATT&CK.

script.intro: Hello, and welcome to Incident response. This is the seminar where everything comes together. Garnet Precision Engineering makes parts in Chakan, near Pune. Just after midnight on Saturday the seventh of November 2026, the helpdesk logs that the engineering CAD files won't open, and every folder has a new file called RESTORE-FILES.txt. That's ransomware. Over the next twenty minutes we'll do what a real incident team does: take custody of the evidence, find out what happened, rebuild the night on one timeline, follow the attacker's hands through the process tree and the computer's memory, name every step in a shared language, make the hard decisions, and write a report for two very different readers: the managing director and the technical team. Let's begin the way every investigation should begin, before reading a single word: with custody.

steps.say: Step one: take custody of the evidence. If this case ever reaches the police, an insurer or a court, someone will ask whether the evidence was changed after you received it. Two things answer that question. Hashes, the fingerprint of each file. And a chain of custody, a log of who handled which file, when, and what its hash was. The Linux cell lists and hashes every file. Then in the Hex tool we open the ransom note, hash it, and add a custody entry.
steps.after: Sixteen files, including the README and the tabletop exercise, each with its SHA-256 hash. In the Hex tool the ransom note's hash starts 2958bfbf. A custody entry says what you did, received from IT, hashed, or copied for analysis, when you did it, and who you are. Add one for the ransom note and one for the malware's strings file, then download the chain of custody. It feels like paperwork, and it is, but it's the paperwork that makes the rest of your work count. Answer the questions: sixteen files, and 2958bfbf.

steps.say: Step two: what happened, in one look. Start from the damage and work backwards. We read three files: the ransom note, the listing of the encrypted share, and the backup report. From them, write down three facts: what was encrypted, when it started, and what is left to restore from.
steps.after: The ransom note says every file now ends in .garnet-locked, the backups and shadow copies are gone, and then the line that changes everything: we also copied 1.8 gigabytes of your engineering drawings, and if you don't pay within 72 hours we publish them. That's double extortion: encryption and a threat to leak. The share listing shows the first files renamed at 23:42 UTC on Friday night. And the backup report: the nightly backup to the NAS ran at 21:00, but the NAS share was reachable from fs02, so it's encrypted too. The shadow copies were deleted at 23:41. The weekly tape from Thursday was taken off site and was test-restored on Friday morning, so the tape survives. Restoring 2.1 terabytes from tape will take about fourteen hours, and everything saved after Thursday at 21:00 is lost unless it exists somewhere else. Answer the questions: .garnet-locked, 23:42, and tape.

steps.say: Step three: rebuild the night on one timeline. Every system keeps its own log, and none of them tells the whole story. The merged timeline reads the VPN log, both Windows machines' event logs and the process export, and sorts every event by time. Narrow it to 22:40 on Friday through midnight, and star the events that tell the story. The VPN log and Windows both use UTC, so they line up directly.
steps.after: Read the starred events in order. 22:43, a failed VPN login for s.kale from 203.0.113.140, bad password. 22:44:10, a successful login for the same account, and MFA says not enrolled. That's the way in: one password, no second factor, on the account of Sachin Kale, a design engineer who, HR tells us, has been on medical leave at home in Nashik all week. 22:52, eng-ws14, a design workstation, logs a remote desktop logon for s.kale from the VPN's address. 23:05, Sysmon records rundll32 opening lsass, the process that holds logged-in users' credentials, with full access. 23:20:03, fs02, the file server, logs a network logon from ENG-WS14 as adm.rjoshi, an administrator. Six seconds later fs02 installs a new service. 23:41, the shadow copies are deleted. 23:42, the encryption. Download the timeline when you've starred it. Answer the questions: 22:44:10, and s.kale.

steps.say: Step four: the process tree, from a shell to the keys. Every program has a parent, and the process tree shows who started what, so you can follow the attacker's hands on each machine. The tool flags the usual warning signs: programs running from folders anyone can write to, hidden PowerShell, downloads, and anything that deletes backups.
steps.after: On eng-ws14, inside s.kale's remote desktop session, a cmd.exe starts at 22:54. Then, one after another: whoami slash groups, who am I and what can I do. net group Domain Admins, who are the most powerful accounts. nltest dclist, where are the domain controllers. That's the attacker looking around. At 22:58, PowerShell with a hidden window downloads r.zip from 203.0.113.140 into C:\Users\Public and unpacks it: a toolkit. At 23:05, rundll32 calls comsvcs.dll with the MiniDump function to write lsass's memory to a file. comsvcs.dll is a real Windows file, already on every machine, which is exactly why attackers like it. At 23:12, nt.exe from the toolkit reads that dump. At 23:19, px.exe connects to fs02 as adm.rjoshi. On fs02, a service called WinUpdSvc copies locker.exe across from eng-ws14 and runs it. Mark every attacker process. Answer the questions: comsvcs.dll, and WinUpdSvc.

steps.say: Step five: memory, what the RAM remembered. The incident team took a memory image of eng-ws14 at 01:14 and ran Volatility on it, the standard tool for reading memory. We can't run Volatility in the browser, but we can read its saved output. Memory shows things logs can miss: processes that have already exited, their full command lines, network connections, and who was logged in to which session.
steps.after: lsass is PID 724. rundll32, PID 6630, ran comsvcs.dll MiniDump 724 to a file called lsass.dmp, and exited fourteen seconds later. nt.exe read lsass.dmp to pull out the passwords and hashes inside it. And px.exe's command line shows the prize: it connects to 10.50.1.12, which is fs02, as GARNET backslash adm.rjoshi, with minus H followed by an NTLM hash. Minus H means it's using the password hash itself, not the password. That's called pass the hash: if you have the hash, you don't need to crack it. The sessions list shows the attacker in RDP session 3 as s.kale, and a separate console session 1 for n.gokhale, the engineer who was really at that desk earlier in the evening. Answer the questions: lsass is PID 724, the account was adm.rjoshi, and the session was 3.

steps.say: Step six: the file server, how they arrived. On fs02 the same night looks like an administrator logging on over the network and installing a service, which administrators do all the time. So we have to read the details. First fs02's own Security and System logs in the event viewer, then the output of two tools the team captured: Hayabusa, which scans event logs for known attack patterns, and Velociraptor, which lists the services.
steps.after: At 23:20:03, adm.rjoshi logs on to fs02 from 10.50.2.14, which is eng-ws14, with Logon Type 3, over the network, and the authentication package is NTLM. An administrator on this domain normally uses Kerberos. NTLM, from a design workstation, at 23:20 on a Friday, six seconds before a brand new service: that's the pass-the-hash pattern. Event 4672 shows special privileges assigned, and 5140 shows the ADMIN dollar share used to copy the file. The System log's 7045 says WinUpdSvc was installed, a name made to look like Windows Update. Hayabusa flags two critical findings: shadow copies deleted with vssadmin delete shadows slash all slash quiet, and a mass file rename, 1,842 files in sixty seconds, with the .garnet-locked extension. Velociraptor confirms WinUpdSvc's path. Answer the questions: 10.50.2.14, and vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet.

steps.say: Step seven: map the attack to ATT&CK. MITRE ATT&CK gives each attacker behaviour a shared name and number, so a reader at another company, at the insurer or at CERT-In knows exactly what you mean without a long explanation. We map every step on the timeline to one technique, with the evidence that proves it, and mark them on the heatmap.
steps.after: Read the table on your screen. The VPN login with a valid account and no MFA is T1133, external remote services, and T1078, valid accounts. The remote desktop hop is T1021.001. whoami, net group and nltest are discovery, T1087.002 and T1018. The hidden PowerShell download is T1105 and T1059.001. Dumping lsass is T1003.001, credential dumping. Using adm.rjoshi's hash over SMB is T1550.002, pass the hash, and T1021.002. The service is T1569.002. Deleting shadow copies is T1490, inhibit system recovery. And the encryption plus the leak threat are T1486 and T1657. Now the question at the bottom: which one step, if blocked, would have stopped everything else? Look at the very first row. MFA on the VPN. The attacker had one password and nothing else. Answer the question: Inhibit System Recovery is T1490.

steps.say: Step eight: decide under pressure. Responders make calls before they have all the facts, and every call costs time. Play the tabletop as the incident lead first. Each choice moves the clock, and the debrief at the end says what good looks like. Then play it again as the managing director, and notice which decision is hardest from that seat.
steps.after: The best path scores ten. The first call: pull the network cable, cut the VPN session, and keep the machines powered on. Isolate, don't power off, because memory is evidence, and you've just seen how much the memory image told us. The other calls: don't restore before the way in is closed, or the attacker simply comes back. Start the CERT-In clock correctly: the tabletop says Garnet noticed at 00:31 UTC, when the incident team was called, so the report is due by 06:31 UTC, with what you know, not six hours after the investigation finishes. Treat the 1.8 gigabytes as stolen until you can show otherwise. And the managing director's hardest call is usually the ransom. Write one line for each decision on why you made it.

steps.say: Step nine: write the executive summary and the technical annex. One report, two readers. The summary section is for the managing director: half a page, no jargon, ending with the decisions needed today. The rest is the technical annex for IT, the insurer and CERT-In, with the timeline, the scope and the lessons.
steps.after: Read the model summary as if you were the managing director at eight on a Saturday morning. It says what happened in plain words: someone logged in remotely with an engineer's password, reached the file server, encrypted the engineering share and says they copied drawings. It says what's been done, what it means for Monday, and what's needed today: approve the restore from Thursday's tape, approve the CERT-In report, decide who talks to customers. Is pass the hash in it? No, and it shouldn't be. The annex has the UTC timeline, the ATT&CK table, and the scope: what was affected, and also what was checked and found clean. And each lesson leads to an action with an owner, starting with MFA for every VPN account.

steps.say: Step ten: hand in. Hand in this notebook: every answer, every tool result, the chain of custody, the timeline and the report. Your teacher marks it with the rubric, and your certificate follows.
steps.after: Before you press Hand in, read your summary one last time as the managing director, and your timeline one last time as the insurer. If either of them would need to call you to understand it, fix that first.

script.outro: That's a full incident, from custody to the boardroom. One password with no second factor let an attacker into the VPN. A remote desktop, a few discovery commands, a credential dump with a tool that's already on every Windows machine, a stolen administrator hash, a fake service, deleted shadow copies, and an encrypted share with a threat to leak. You traced every step through logs, the process tree and memory, named it in ATT&CK, made the calls in the right order, and wrote it for two readers. The lessons that matter most: isolate, don't switch off; close the way in before you restore; start the CERT-In clock when you noticed; and turn on MFA everywhere it's missing. Next, in Breach clocks, we go deeper into exactly who you have to tell, and by when. Thank you for watching.

template.s:
# Incident response: ransomware, lateral movement and memory (Practice)

Practice: the same Garnet ransomware night, with fewer hints and harder questions. Most answers need you to follow one fact from a log into another file.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `backups.txt`, `captured/hayabusa-fs02.csv`, `captured/velociraptor-fs02-services.csv`, `captured/volatility-eng-ws14.txt`, `eventlogs/eng-ws14-Security.jsonl`, `eventlogs/eng-ws14-Sysmon.jsonl`, `eventlogs/fs02-Security.jsonl`, `eventlogs/fs02-System.jsonl`, `hr_note.txt`, `process.csv`, `README.txt`, `share_listing.txt`, `suspect/locker.strings.txt`, `suspect/RESTORE-FILES.txt`, `tabletop-garnet-ransomware.json`, `vpn.log`.

## 1. Take custody of the evidence

Before you read anything, hash it, and start a **chain of custody**: who handled which file, when, and what its hash was. If this ends up with the police, an insurer or a court, the custody log is what makes your evidence count.

```tool hex
{"file": "suspect/RESTORE-FILES.txt", "sha256": "", "n": 0, "custody": [], "blank": ["sha256"], "a": {"sha256": "2958bfbf3ed6df5ef7f177fa6e8307fe21efb29172e73470fdc5aaa949659ad7"}}
```

- [ ] Hash every file (the Linux cell)
- [ ] In the Hex tool, open the ransom note, hash it and add a custody entry
- [ ] Add a custody entry for locker.strings.txt too
- [ ] Download the chain of custody

?> At what UTC time (HH:MM) was the memory image of eng-ws14 taken? :: sha256:ec755ac4018ba9f6af957e7d9d13016298db8b6e8f08dfe04185d1ca982f3a20

?> How many minutes after the helpdesk ticket was the incident team called? :: sha256:9400f1b21cb527d7fa3d3eabba93557a18ebe7a2ca4e471cfe5e4c5b4ca7f767

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with find.
template.a:
cd ~/case
find . -type f | sort
echo ---
find . -type f -exec sha256sum {} + | sort -k2

template.s:
## 2. What happened, in one look

Start from the damage and work backwards. Read the ransom note, the share listing and the backup report. Write down three facts: what was encrypted, when it started, and what is left to restore from.

- [ ] Which extension do the encrypted files have?
- [ ] When was the first file renamed?
- [ ] What does the attacker claim besides encryption?
- [ ] Which backup survived, and how much work will be lost?

?> On which date did the tape backup you can restore from run? (YYYY-MM-DD) :: sha256:cd3af2c65bc838d00637730aa75aa2389d0873d6dc560ca2017ccd9da51f1bc4

?> How many hours does the restore from tape take? :: sha256:8527a891e224136950ff32ca212b45bc93f69fbb801c3b1ebedac52775f99e61

?> How many files does the audit count say were renamed? :: sha256:3ab57220f1f10003766dcc4180152b17dfdd7cc9f4e5ccdecf5b48df25ae861c

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with cat.
template.a:
cd ~/case
cat suspect/RESTORE-FILES.txt
echo ---
cat share_listing.txt
echo ---
cat backups.txt

template.s:
## 3. Rebuild the night on one timeline

Put every log on one clock. The merged timeline reads the VPN log, both machines' event logs and the process export together, sorted by time. Star the events that tell the story; the gaps tell you something too.

```tool timeline
{"keys": "", "n": 7, "blank": ["keys"], "a": {"keys": ["vpn.log#6@1794005050", "eventlogs/eng-ws14-Security.jsonl#4@1794005551", "eventlogs/eng-ws14-Sysmon.jsonl#8@1794006344", "eventlogs/fs02-Security.jsonl#5@1794007203", "eventlogs/fs02-System.jsonl#1@1794007209", "process.csv#17@1794008461", "process.csv#19@1794008530"]}}
```

- [ ] When did the attacker get in, and through what?
- [ ] When did they reach eng-ws14, and how?
- [ ] When did they reach fs02, and as whom?
- [ ] Star the key events and download the timeline

?> From which outside IP address did the s.kale VPN login come? :: sha256:63e456fc357cb014cf8712fcd1958fa41f051d4e4dc0ff5ddd627d20fadf0cc2

?> Which file did the attacker download from that same address? (file name) :: sha256:b4ec68ef759ea6d2c2ba0ff403068367931cebcefff4d9f5e60c4aed05da8dc9

## 4. The process tree: from a shell to the keys

Every program has a parent. The process tree shows who started what, so you can follow the attacker's hands on each machine. The tool flags the usual tells: programs in folders anyone can write to, hidden PowerShell, downloads, deleting backups.

```tool proctree
{"marks": "", "n": 14, "files": ["process.csv"], "blank": ["marks"], "a": {"marks": ["eng-ws14|6344", "eng-ws14|6402", "eng-ws14|6418", "eng-ws14|6440", "eng-ws14|6511", "eng-ws14|6630", "eng-ws14|6711", "eng-ws14|6790", "fs02|4410", "fs02|4422", "fs02|4512", "fs02|4514", "fs02|4530", "fs02|4601"]}}
```

- [ ] On eng-ws14: what did the attacker run from the RDP session's cmd.exe, in order?
- [ ] Which process read lsass's memory, and with which DLL?
- [ ] On fs02: what started the encryption, and what ran just before it?
- [ ] Mark every attacker process

?> Which program read the lsass dump? (file name) :: sha256:bdda0a3709213b25ad3bc40101d96a4fc6bffa8a1db74d3f73db68c9e9a624d3

?> What are the last 8 characters of the hash px.exe passed? :: sha256:b645667a8ab6543d916ea39df385400f62f697c3c1d3739050cb96ecb5dd5a99

## 5. Memory: what the RAM remembered

The incident team took a memory image of eng-ws14 at 01:14 and ran Volatility on it. We can't re-run Volatility in the browser, but we can read its saved output. Memory shows things logs can miss: exited processes, the command lines, network connections and who was in which session.

- [ ] Which PID is lsass, and which process dumped it?
- [ ] What did nt.exe do with the dump?
- [ ] Which account and password hash did px.exe use, against which server?
- [ ] Which session were they in, and whose was the other one?

?> What is the parent PID of lsass.exe? :: sha256:55f0124bb79f5c53d868ca45bbb0f4d04da15eea4fb29c6b95087fe8801bf0a3

?> Which local port did px.exe use for its connection to fs02? :: sha256:d70d4bf89f0fa597d6998cd707626b5c148a3307df7d3eacd021cd524fe6f104

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with grep.
template.a:
cd ~/case/captured
grep -E '^(724|6630|6711|6790) ' volatility-eng-ws14.txt
echo ---
grep -A4 'windows.cmdline' volatility-eng-ws14.txt
echo ---
grep -A4 'windows.sessions' volatility-eng-ws14.txt

template.s:
## 6. The file server: how they arrived

On fs02 the same night looks like an administrator logging on over the network and installing a service. Read it in fs02's own logs, then compare with the Hayabusa and Velociraptor output the team captured.

```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/fs02-Security.jsonl", "ids": "", "q": "", "n": 3, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "4624, 4672, 5140", "q": "adm.rjoshi"}}
```

```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/fs02-System.jsonl", "ids": "", "n": 1, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "7045"}}
```

- [ ] When did adm.rjoshi log on, from where, with which package (Kerberos or NTLM)?
- [ ] Which share was used to copy the service file?
- [ ] Which service was installed, running as whom?
- [ ] What did Hayabusa flag as critical?

?> How many seconds after the network logon was the WinUpdSvc service installed? :: sha256:e7f6c011776e8db7cd330b54174fd76f7d0216b612387a5ffcfb81e6f0919683

?> Which program turned off boot recovery? (file name) :: sha256:f617bb5448f2209725f995863751e1bd2016ac6553585ed0b98b6fc13b954502

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with cut.
template.a:
cd ~/case/captured
cut -d, -f1-3 hayabusa-fs02.csv
echo ---
grep -i 'crit' hayabusa-fs02.csv | cut -d, -f2,8
echo ---
grep -i winupd velociraptor-fs02-services.csv

## 7. Map the attack to ATT&CK

ATT&CK gives each step a shared name, so a reader at another company, an insurer or CERT-In knows exactly what you mean. Map every step on your timeline to one technique, with the evidence that proves it.

```tool ioc
{"attack": "", "blank": ["iocs", "attack"], "a": {"attack": ["T1133", "T1078", "T1021.001", "T1087.002", "T1018", "T1105", "T1059.001", "T1003.001", "T1550.002", "T1021.002", "T1569.002", "T1490", "T1486", "T1657"]}}
```

| Time (UTC) | Step | Technique | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22:44 | VPN login with a valid account, no MFA | T1133, T1078 | vpn.log |
| 22:52 | RDP to eng-ws14 | T1021.001 | eng-ws14 4624 type 10 |
| 22:54 | whoami, net group, nltest | T1087.002, T1018 | process.csv |
| 22:58 | Toolkit downloaded with hidden PowerShell | T1105, T1059.001 | process.csv |
| 23:05 | lsass dumped with comsvcs.dll | T1003.001 | Sysmon 1, 10, 11; Volatility |
| 23:20 | adm.rjoshi's hash used on fs02 over SMB | T1550.002, T1021.002 | fs02 4624 NTLM, 5140 ADMIN$ |
| 23:20 | Service WinUpdSvc runs the payload | T1569.002 | 7045; Velociraptor |
| 23:41 | Shadow copies deleted, recovery off | T1490 | Hayabusa; process.csv |
| 23:42 | Share encrypted, extortion note | T1486, T1657 | share_listing.txt; note |

- [ ] Every row has a technique and a piece of evidence
- [ ] Mark the techniques on the heatmap
- [ ] Which one step, if blocked, would have stopped the rest?

?> Which ATT&CK technique ID is the LSASS memory dump? (with the sub-technique) :: sha256:c52272349a4285d697459a4eb2abb0bd60660389a5dc94b48ba37eb64c9c8721

## 8. Decide under pressure

Responders make calls before they have all the facts. Play the tabletop as the incident lead. Each choice costs time; the debrief at the end says what good looks like.

```tool tabletop
{"file": "tabletop-garnet-ransomware.json", "path": "", "n": 10, "blank": ["path"], "a": {"path": [{"node": "t1", "c": 0, "label": "Pull the network cable, cut the VPN session, keep the machines powered on"}, {"node": "t2", "c": 0, "label": "Don't pay; restore from the Thursday tape; get legal advice on the customer contracts"}, {"node": "t3", "c": 0, "label": "File with CERT-In by 06:31 UTC with what we know, and update later"}, {"node": "t4", "c": 0, "label": "Turn on MFA for every VPN account and reset s.kale and adm.rjoshi before bringing fs02 back"}, {"node": "t5", "c": 0, "label": "Tell staff and the affected customer plainly what happened and what you are doing"}]}}
```

- [ ] Play it once as the incident lead
- [ ] Play it again as the managing director: which call is hardest from that seat?
- [ ] For each decision, one line on why

?> What is the best score you can get in the tabletop? :: sha256:4a44dc15364204a80fe80e9039455cc1608281820fe2b24f1e5233ade6af1dd5

## 9. Write the executive summary and the technical annex

Two readers, one report. The **Summary** section is the executive summary: half a page a managing director can act on, with the decisions needed today. The rest is the technical annex for IT, the insurer and CERT-In.

```tool report
{"tpl": "incident", "title": "Incident report: ransomware at Garnet Precision Engineering, 6 to 7 November 2026", "text": "", "n": 9, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Incident report: ransomware at Garnet Precision Engineering, 6 to 7 November 2026

## Summary

On Friday night an outsider logged in to our VPN with an engineer's password, because that account had no second factor. Within an hour they took an administrator's credentials from a design workstation, used them on the file server, deleted the recovery copies and encrypted 1,842 files in the Engineering and Quality shares. They claim to have copied 1.8 GB of drawings. We contained it at 01:10 on Saturday, nothing else is known to be affected, and we are restoring from Thursday's off-site tape (about 14 hours; Friday's work is lost). Decisions needed today: do not pay; approve MFA on every VPN account now; approve telling the affected automotive customer today.

## Timeline

All times UTC. 22:43 VPN login fails for s.kale from 203.0.113.140; 22:44:10 succeeds, no MFA. 22:52:31 RDP to eng-ws14 (type 10 logon). 22:54 to 22:58 discovery and toolkit download. 23:05:44 lsass dumped with comsvcs.dll. 23:20:03 adm.rjoshi logs on to fs02 with NTLM from eng-ws14; 23:20:09 service WinUpdSvc installed. 23:41 shadow copies deleted, boot recovery disabled. 23:42:10 locker.exe starts; 23:42:31 first files renamed. 00:12 helpdesk ticket; 00:31 incident team; 00:58 VPN session cut; 01:10 both machines isolated.

## Scope

Affected: eng-ws14 (RDP session, credential dump), fs02 (encryption of D:\Shares, 1,842 files), nas01 backup share (encrypted from fs02). Accounts: s.kale (password), adm.rjoshi (NTLM hash). Not seen: dc01 logons by the attacker, other workstations. The VPN session moved 1.84 GB out, which fits the claim of copied drawings.

## Impact

Engineering and Quality shares unavailable until restored; work from Friday lost; possible publication of customer drawings (confidential under the customer contract). No personal data is known to be in those shares; HR confirms.

## Root cause

A VPN that accepts a password alone, and an administrator who had logged on to a workstation, leaving a reusable credential in lsass memory.

## Containment, eradication and recovery

Done: VPN session cut, both machines isolated, s.kale and adm.rjoshi disabled. Next: rebuild eng-ws14 and fs02 from clean images; reset all admin passwords and the krbtgt key twice; MFA on every VPN account; restore from tape; administrators use separate admin workstations only.

## Who was told, and when

Managing director 00:45; CERT-In report due by 06:31 UTC (six hours from 00:31); cyber insurer 02:00; the automotive customer today; staff at 09:00.

## Indicators

203.0.113.140 (VPN source, toolkit download); C:\Users\Public\r\ (nt.exe, px.exe, locker.exe); service WinUpdSvc; C:\ProgramData\gpe\locker.exe; extension .garnet-locked; support-desk@onion-mail[.]example.

## Lessons learned

One missing control (MFA on the VPN) opened the door; one habit (admins logging on to ordinary workstations) handed over the keys. The off-site tape is why we can recover at all.
```
